easy.text: What does 'accuracy' mean in scientific measurement?

options.text: How close a measurement is to the true or accepted value
options.feedback: Correct -- an accurate measurement is close to the actual, correct value.

options.text: How many times you repeat a measurement
options.feedback: Repetition count relates to gathering data, not the definition of accuracy itself.

options.text: How expensive the measuring equipment is
options.feedback: Equipment cost isn't what determines accuracy -- closeness to the true value is.

options.text: How quickly a measurement can be taken
options.feedback: Speed of measurement isn't related to the concept of accuracy.

medium.text: A set of measurements are all very close to each other, but far from the true value. What does this describe?

options.text: Precise but not accurate
options.feedback: Correct -- precision refers to consistency between measurements, regardless of whether they're actually correct.

options.text: Accurate but not precise
options.feedback: This is backwards -- being consistently close together (regardless of correctness) describes precision, not accuracy.

options.text: Both accurate and precise
options.feedback: Since the measurements are far from the true value, they can't be considered accurate, even though they're precise.

options.text: Neither accurate nor precise
options.feedback: The measurements ARE precise (consistent with each other), even though they aren't accurate.

hard.text: Why is it possible for a set of measurements to be precise but not accurate, using a scale as an example?

options.text: A scale could be consistently miscalibrated, giving the same (wrong) reading every time
options.feedback: Correct -- a systematic error, like a miscalibrated scale, produces consistent (precise) results that are all off from the true value (inaccurate).

options.text: This situation is actually impossible in real measurements
options.feedback: This is a well-documented, common measurement scenario, not an impossibility.

options.text: Precise measurements are always automatically accurate
options.feedback: Precision and accuracy are independent qualities -- consistent results can still all be systematically wrong.

options.text: The measurer must have made a different random mistake every single time
options.feedback: Random, different mistakes each time would actually reduce precision (consistency), not preserve it -- a systematic, consistent error explains this scenario better.

easy.hard: This quality reflects how near a result is to the actual correct answer.
easy.medium: This describes how close your answer is to the real, correct value.
easy.easy: This is how close a measurement is to the real, correct answer.

medium.hard: One term describes closeness to the true value; the other describes consistency among repeated measurements, regardless of correctness.
medium.medium: Being close together each time, even if wrong, describes one specific measurement quality.
medium.easy: Being consistent every time, even if wrong, is called being precise.

hard.hard: A consistent systematic error (like incorrect calibration) reliably shifts every reading by the same amount, preserving precision (consistency) while destroying accuracy (correctness).
hard.medium: If a scale is set up wrong from the start, it'll give the same wrong number every time -- consistent, but consistently incorrect.
hard.easy: If a scale is broken in a consistent way, it gives the same wrong answer every time -- consistent, but wrong.

easy.text: What are significant figures used for in a measurement?

options.text: Indicating how precisely a value was measured
options.feedback: Correct -- significant figures communicate the certainty/precision behind a reported number.

options.text: Showing the color of the substance measured
options.feedback: Significant figures relate to numerical precision, not color.

options.text: Indicating the temperature of the room
options.feedback: Significant figures aren't tied to room temperature -- they reflect measurement precision.

options.text: Showing how much the equipment costs
options.feedback: Equipment cost isn't related to the concept of significant figures.

medium.text: How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.0450?

options.feedback: Correct -- leading zeros don't count, but the trailing zero after the decimal does, giving 4, 5, and 0 as significant.
This counts the leading zeros, which aren't significant.
This misses counting the significant trailing zero after the decimal point.
This overcounts by including a zero that shouldn't be counted.

hard.text: Why does a measurement of 12.0 mL imply greater precision than a measurement of 12 mL, even though they represent the same approximate quantity?

options.text: The trailing zero after the decimal point signals the measurement was made to the tenths place, implying more precise instrumentation
options.feedback: Correct -- writing 12.0 communicates confidence down to the tenths digit, while 12 alone leaves that precision ambiguous.

options.text: 12.0 mL is actually a larger volume than 12 mL
options.feedback: These represent the same actual volume -- the difference is only in the implied precision of measurement, not the quantity itself.

options.text: There is no real difference in meaning between the two
options.feedback: In scientific notation conventions, the trailing zero specifically conveys additional precision information.

options.text: 12 mL was measured using a more advanced instrument
options.feedback: This has it backwards -- the version WITH the decimal (12.0) is the one implying more precise instrumentation, not the whole number alone.

easy.hard: This convention communicates how confidently precise a recorded numerical value is.
easy.medium: This tells you how carefully or precisely a measurement was actually taken.
easy.easy: This shows how precisely a number was actually measured.

medium.hard: Leading zeros before the first nonzero digit are never significant, but zeros appearing after the decimal point, following other digits, generally are.
medium.medium: Zeros at the very beginning don't count, but zeros after the decimal point following other digits usually do.
medium.easy: The leading zeros don't count, but the last zero after the decimal does -- count 4, 5, and 0.

hard.hard: A trailing zero written explicitly after a decimal point is a deliberate signal of measured precision to that decimal place, distinguishing it from an implied, less-precise whole number.
hard.medium: Writing the extra zero after the decimal point tells you the measurement was actually taken carefully down to that level of detail.
hard.easy: Writing the extra .0 tells you the measurement was actually checked down to that level of detail.

topic: Charles's Law (temperature and volume of gases)

easy.text: According to Charles's Law, what happens to a gas's volume when its temperature increases (at constant pressure)?

options.text: The volume increases
options.feedback: Correct -- temperature and volume have a direct relationship at constant pressure.

options.text: The volume decreases
options.feedback: This is the opposite of Charles's Law's direct relationship -- higher temperature means larger volume.

options.text: The volume stays exactly the same
options.feedback: Charles's Law specifically describes how volume changes with temperature -- it doesn't stay constant.

options.text: The gas turns into a liquid
options.feedback: Simple heating under normal conditions causes expansion, not necessarily a state change to liquid.

medium.text: A balloon is placed in a hot car and expands as the temperature rises. If the balloon isn't perfectly rigid, why does this expansion happen?

options.text: The gas molecules inside move faster and spread further apart as temperature increases, at roughly constant pressure
options.feedback: Correct -- increased molecular motion pushes the flexible balloon walls outward, increasing volume.

options.text: The rubber material itself chemically changes and grows
options.feedback: The rubber material doesn't fundamentally change -- it's the gas inside expanding that stretches the balloon.

options.text: Cold air from outside enters and pushes the balloon out
options.feedback: This scenario involves the car getting hot, not cold air entering -- the expansion is due to internal gas heating.

options.text: The balloon loses mass, making it larger
options.feedback: Losing mass wouldn't cause expansion -- the balloon expands because the trapped gas's volume increases with temperature.

hard.text: A gas occupies 2 liters at 300 K. If the temperature increases to 450 K (at constant pressure), what is the new volume? (Use V1/T1 = V2/T2)

options.text: 3 liters
2.5 liters
options.feedback: This doesn't match correctly solving the proportional relationship.

options.text: 1.5 liters
options.feedback: This decreases instead of increasing the volume, contrary to Charles's Law's direct relationship.

options.text: 4.5 liters
options.feedback: This overstates the correct proportional increase.

easy.hard: Temperature and volume move in the SAME direction as each other, unlike the inverse relationship in Boyle's Law.
easy.medium: As temperature goes up, volume goes up too, if pressure stays the same.
easy.easy: Heating a gas usually makes it expand and take up more space.

medium.hard: Higher temperature increases the average kinetic energy and speed of gas particles, causing them to occupy more space when free to expand.
medium.medium: The gas particles move faster and spread out more as they heat up, pushing the flexible balloon outward.
medium.easy: As the gas inside heats up, its particles spread out more, pushing the balloon bigger.

hard.hard: Set up the ratio of volume to temperature as equal before and after the change, then solve for the unknown volume.
hard.medium: Multiply 2 by 450, then divide by 300 to find the new volume.

topic: activation energy and reaction energy diagrams

options.text: The minimum energy needed to start a chemical reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- reactants need to reach this energy threshold before a reaction can proceed.

options.text: The total energy released by a reaction
options.feedback: That describes the overall energy change of the reaction, not specifically the activation energy needed to start it.

options.text: The energy needed to freeze a substance
options.feedback: Freezing relates to a physical state change, not the chemical concept of activation energy.

options.text: The weight of the reactants
options.feedback: Weight/mass is unrelated to the energy concept of activation energy.

medium.text: On a reaction energy diagram, what does the peak (highest point) of the curve represent?

options.text: The transition state, where the energy is at its maximum during the reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- this peak represents the highest-energy, most unstable arrangement as reactants become products.

options.text: The starting energy of the reactants
options.feedback: That's shown at the beginning of the curve, not at its peak.

options.text: The final energy of the products
options.feedback: That's shown at the end of the curve, not at its peak.

options.text: The temperature of the room during the reaction
options.feedback: Room temperature isn't represented on this type of energy diagram -- it tracks reaction progress versus energy.

hard.text: A catalyst is added to a reaction. How does this change the reaction's energy diagram?

options.text: It lowers the height of the activation energy peak, without changing the starting or ending energy levels
options.feedback: Correct -- catalysts provide an alternate pathway with a lower energy barrier, but don't change the overall energy released or absorbed.

options.text: It raises the activation energy peak
options.feedback: Catalysts specifically LOWER the activation energy barrier, making the reaction easier, not harder.

options.text: It changes the final energy level of the products
options.feedback: A catalyst doesn't change the overall energy difference between reactants and products -- only the pathway/barrier height.

options.text: It has no effect on the energy diagram at all
options.feedback: A catalyst does visibly change the diagram by lowering the activation energy peak.

easy.hard: This threshold must be overcome before reactants can successfully transform into products.
easy.medium: This is the energy "barrier" that needs to be crossed to get a reaction going.
easy.easy: This is the minimum energy needed to kick-start a reaction.

medium.hard: This highest point corresponds to a temporary, high-energy, unstable molecular arrangement partway through bond breaking/forming.
medium.medium: This is the point of highest energy the reacting molecules pass through partway through the reaction.
medium.easy: This is the highest point the energy reaches partway through the reaction.

hard.hard: A catalyst opens an alternate reaction pathway with a reduced energy barrier, without altering the thermodynamic energy difference between reactants and products.
hard.medium: A catalyst makes it easier to reach the peak of the energy diagram, without changing where the reaction starts or ends energy-wise.
hard.easy: A catalyst just makes the peak of the energy diagram lower and easier to reach.

options.text: A solid changing directly into a gas, without becoming a liquid first
options.feedback: Correct -- dry ice (solid CO₂) is a classic example of sublimation.

options.text: A gas changing directly into a solid
options.feedback: That's the reverse process, called deposition, not sublimation.

options.text: A liquid changing into a gas
options.feedback: That's evaporation, a different process from sublimation.

options.text: A solid changing into a liquid
options.feedback: That's melting, a different process from sublimation.

medium.text: What is deposition, in terms of state changes?

options.text: A gas changing directly into a solid, without becoming a liquid first
options.feedback: Correct -- deposition is the reverse of sublimation, like frost forming directly from water vapor.

options.text: A solid changing directly into a gas
options.feedback: That's sublimation, the reverse process of deposition.

options.text: A liquid freezing into a solid
options.feedback: That's freezing, a different process from deposition.

options.text: A gas condensing into a liquid
options.feedback: That's condensation, a different process from deposition.

hard.text: Frost sometimes forms directly on a cold window on a humid night, without any visible liquid water appearing first. Which process does this best illustrate?

options.text: Deposition -- water vapor in the air converts directly into solid ice on the cold surface
options.feedback: Correct -- when water vapor contacts a surface cold enough, it can skip the liquid phase entirely and form solid ice crystals directly.

options.text: Sublimation -- ice on the window turns directly into vapor
options.feedback: This scenario describes vapor turning INTO solid frost, the opposite direction from sublimation.

options.text: Melting -- solid ice turns into liquid water
options.feedback: No ice-to-liquid transition is occurring here -- frost is forming directly from vapor, not melting.

options.text: Boiling -- liquid water rapidly turns into vapor
options.feedback: Boiling requires a liquid, but no liquid water is involved in this direct vapor-to-solid frost formation.

easy.hard: This process skips the intermediate liquid state entirely, going straight from rigid to diffuse.
easy.medium: This is when something goes straight from solid to gas, skipping the liquid stage.
easy.easy: This is when a solid turns straight into gas, skipping being a liquid.

medium.hard: This process skips the intermediate liquid state entirely, going straight from diffuse to rigid.
medium.medium: This is when something goes straight from gas to solid, skipping the liquid stage.
medium.easy: This is when a gas turns straight into a solid, skipping being a liquid.

hard.hard: Water vapor molecules losing enough energy upon contact with a sufficiently cold surface can crystallize directly into solid ice, bypassing the liquid phase.
hard.medium: The water vapor in the air is cooling down so fast on the cold glass that it turns straight into ice crystals, skipping the liquid stage.
hard.easy: The water vapor in the air turns straight into ice on the cold glass, without ever being a liquid first.

options.text: A solution that has dissolved the maximum amount of solute possible at that temperature
options.feedback: Correct -- a saturated solution is at its dissolving limit under the current conditions.

options.text: A solution with no solute dissolved at all
options.feedback: That would just be pure solvent, not a saturated solution.

options.text: A solution that has been boiled
options.feedback: Boiling isn't what defines saturation -- the amount of dissolved solute relative to the maximum possible does.

options.text: A solution that is always colored
options.feedback: Color isn't relevant to whether a solution is saturated -- some saturated solutions could be colorless.

options.text: A solution that can still dissolve more solute at that temperature
options.feedback: Correct -- an unsaturated solution hasn't yet reached its maximum dissolving capacity.

options.text: A solution that has already dissolved the maximum amount of solute possible
options.feedback: That describes a saturated solution, not an unsaturated one.

options.text: A solution containing more solute than it should be able to hold
options.feedback: That describes a supersaturated solution, not an unsaturated one.

options.text: A solution with absolutely no water in it
options.feedback: Water content alone doesn't define saturation status -- it's about how much solute has dissolved relative to the maximum.

hard.text: A supersaturated sugar solution is created by dissolving sugar in very hot water, then carefully cooling it without disturbance. Why is this solution unstable?

options.text: It contains more dissolved sugar than the solution could normally hold at that (now cooler) temperature, making it prone to sudden crystallization if disturbed
options.feedback: Correct -- supersaturation is achieved by exceeding the normal solubility limit through careful cooling, but the excess solute can rapidly crystallize out if triggered by a disturbance.

options.text: It actually contains no dissolved sugar at all
options.feedback: A supersaturated solution has MORE dissolved sugar than normal, not none at all.

options.text: It is chemically identical to pure water
options.feedback: It contains a significant amount of dissolved sugar, making it very different from pure water.

options.text: The sugar has permanently changed into a new chemical substance
options.feedback: The sugar is still ordinary sugar -- it's just dissolved in an unusually high, unstable amount for that temperature.

easy.hard: This solution has reached the ceiling of what it can hold under the current conditions.
easy.medium: This solution can't dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
easy.easy: This solution is completely "full" and can't dissolve any more.

medium.hard: This type of solution hasn't yet reached its maximum solute-holding capacity for that temperature.
medium.medium: This solution still has room to dissolve more solute before reaching its limit.
medium.easy: This solution still has room to dissolve more -- it's not "full" yet.

hard.hard: Solubility generally decreases as a solution cools, so a solution that dissolved solute at high temperature and was cooled without disturbance can end up holding more solute than the cooler temperature would normally allow, creating an unstable, easily-triggered excess.
hard.medium: Since solubility usually drops as things cool, this solution ends up holding onto more sugar than it normally could at the cooler temperature -- until something triggers it to suddenly crystallize.
hard.easy: This solution is holding onto more sugar than it normally could at that cooler temperature, so it's ready to suddenly turn solid if disturbed.
